tier_reason: This is a peer-reviewed paper (ALENEX 2014, DOI 10.1137/1.9781611973198.7, confirmed via Semantic Scholar). The code is public (driver/trace_driver.c, run_scripts/, Makefile with gcc -O4), and the Opteron 2212 hardware is stated. But the baseline is the authors' own C implicit binary/d-ary heaps, not std::priority_queue or any shipped library, so it is not an A-grade run against the named baseline.

corrections.baseline: implicit binary heap (the paper's own C implementation, 'implicit 2' / 'implicit simple 2'); std::priority_queue not tested
corrections.claimed_speedup: The pairing heap wins only on some workloads. Table 4, randomized Insert-DeleteMin with c=1024 (a workload the paper itself calls degenerate): pairing 1.00 (fastest) vs implicit 2 11.87, implicit simple 2 11.04, implicit simple 4 6.12, implicit 8 4.90, i.e. ~4.9-11.9x (derived from page data). It LOSES on the standard workloads. Table 3, Dijkstra on the full USA road map: pairing 1.68 vs implicit 2 1.17 and implicit 4 1.00 (pairing ~1.4x slower than the binary heap, derived from page data; the 3.84 the record cited is 'explicit 2', a pointer-based heap). Table 2, sorting: pairing 4.29 vs implicit simple 2 1.59 and implicit simple 4 1.00 (slower), beating only the indirected 'implicit 2' (4.75). The text says workloads with larger heaps (Tables 9, 11, 13-15) favor amortized structures, especially the pairing heap.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc -O4 (repo Makefile: -Wall -g -std=gnu99 -O4); gcc version not stated
corrections.workload: Trace-driven wallclock times normalized to the fastest heap: randomized Insert-DeleteMin with c=1024 (degenerate, stack-like), Dijkstra on the full USA road map, and sorting of uniformly random 64-bit keys, from Larkin/Sen/Tarjan, 'A Back-to-Basics Empirical Study of Priority Queues' (ALENEX 2014).
corrections.caveats: The biggest win (11.87x) is on the insert-delete c=1024 workload, which the paper proves degenerate and calls a 'broken test'. On Dijkstra (USA road map) and sorting the pairing heap is SLOWER than the implicit binary/4-ary heaps. The baseline is the authors' own C binary heap, not std::priority_queue. Hardware is from the 2014 era (Opteron 2212). The repo is an unmaintained auto-export of a shut-down Google Code project (last real commit 2013-09-20, pushed 2015-11-05) with no license file.

notes: The record's Dijkstra figure was wrong: it compared pairing 1.68 to explicit-2 (3.84), not implicit-2 (1.17), so the claimed ~2.3x Dijkstra win is actually a ~1.4x loss. The entry stays because the paper does show real pairing-heap wins on degenerate and large-heap workloads, but it is a research testbed, not a drop-in library.

tier_reason: The paper's Table 1 (arXiv v3 / ESA 2026) gives BinaryHeap 439.6 vs SimdQuickHeapAvx2 35.6 vs Avx512 32.2 ns/elem at n=2^25, and the abstract gives the radix-heap and S3Q ratios. The benchmark code is public (bench/examples/bench.rs via run-all.sh). Rust is built nightly, release, target-cpu=native, fat LTO; C++ competitors use Clang -std=c++17 -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native -flto; the CPU is an AMD EPYC 9684X. The baseline actually run is Rust's std::collections::BinaryHeap.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Table 1, MonotoneConstantSize, i64 keys, n=2^25: SimdQuickHeapAvx2 35.6 ns/elem and SimdQuickHeapAvx512 32.2 ns/elem vs Rust std BinaryHeap 439.6 ns/elem, i.e. ~12.3x and ~13.7x (derived from page data). At small n (2^10) the gap is small: 27.1 / 23.5 vs 27.4 ns/elem. Abstract: 1.2-1.7x as fast as the monotone radix heap (the next-best competitor) and 1.4-2.8x as fast as the superscalar sample queue (S3Q). The README says up to 10x faster than binary and d-ary heaps.
corrections.caveats: Published at ESA 2026 (DOI 10.4230/LIPIcs.ESA.2026.16); very recent, with no independent replication yet. The largest multiplier is against Rust's own BinaryHeap, not libstdc++/libc++/MSVC std::priority_queue (C++ std::priority_queue was not tested; Boost 4-ary heap was). The speedup is small while the heap fits in cache. It supports only i32/u32/i64/u64 keys, needs AVX2 or AVX-512, and the benchmarks need nightly Rust. The C++ bindings are LLM-generated. The repo has no LICENSE file: MIT is declared only in Cargo.toml.

notes: The numbers match the paper exactly; the ratios just needed a 'derived' label. The baseline was relabeled to Rust's BinaryHeap because std::priority_queue itself was never benchmarked. GitHub reports no license (spdx null), but Cargo.toml declares license = "MIT", so it is kept as MIT/copyable with a caveat.

tier_reason: Thesis section 6.5.2 states verbatim that against min(S3QBH, StdQueue) the speedups are 'roughly logarithmic in N for N in [2^13, 2^27], finally reaching values between 4.6 and 7'. StdQueue is GCC's std::priority_queue. The setup is GCC 9.3.0 -O3 on Ubuntu 20.04.2 with a Xeon E5-2650 v2 and an Athlon II X4 635, and the benchmark code is public at benchmarks/benchmark.cpp.in in the repo.
notes: Everything checked out: MIT license, 7 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-05-27. The thesis ran one benchmark copy per physical core to simulate a loaded machine, which is worth keeping in mind when comparing it with single-thread numbers elsewhere.

tier_reason: The README's 'Example results' table (1M ~180ms vs ~320ms, 8M ~1.6s vs ~3.0s, 64M ~15s vs ~28s, '~1.7-2x faster') comes from the project's own Criterion benchmark (benches/benchmark.rs) against Rust std BinaryHeap. The CPU is only described as a 'mid-range desktop CPU' and no compiler version or flags are given, so it is first-party with partial methodology: C.

corrections.workload: Criterion benchmark: push N uniformly random u32 keys, then pop all of them (heapsort pattern), N = 125,000 << i for i in 0..10 (125K-64M), vs Rust std::collections::BinaryHeap<Reverse<u32>>.
corrections.caveats: A university course project (README says Programming in Rust WS 2023/24, two authors, 0 stars). The benchmark is the project's own Criterion suite, with approximate '~' README numbers, no stated CPU model and no compiler flags. It compares only against Rust's std BinaryHeap, never against C++ std::priority_queue. The license is inconsistent: the LICENSE file is Apache-2.0, while the README and Cargo.toml say MIT (both are OSI).

notes: The numbers match the README. The workload was corrected: the benchmark is push-all-then-pop-all, not interleaved. The license is kept as Apache-2.0 because that is what the LICENSE file and GitHub say, and the MIT conflict is noted in caveats.
